title: West Kilbride stargazers see Andromeda and remains of an ancient supernova
excerpt: West Kilbride stargazers viewed the Andromeda Galaxy and Eastern Veil Nebula, a supernova remnant, during Dr Alex MacKinnon's astronomy class in Scotland.
content:
STARGAZERS were treated to spectacular views of deep space as an astronomy class turned its eyes towards the Andromeda Galaxy and the remains of an ancient exploding star.

Members of the Exploring the Universe class, led by lecturer Alex MacKinnon, headed outdoors at West Kilbride Community Centre and braved the cool air for a practical observing session using the naked eye, binoculars and telescopes.

Among the highlights was a view of the Andromeda Galaxy, around 2.5 million light-years from Earth and the nearest major galaxy to our own Milky Way.

The enormous galaxy is estimated to contain around one trillion stars and extend for roughly 152,000 light-years across its readily measured bright disc.

Dr Alexander MacKinnon (Image: University of Glasgow)

It means the light observed by class members had been travelling through space for some 2.5 million years before reaching their eyes.

Another impressive sight came courtesy of a Unistellar smart telescope which produced a striking view of the Eastern Veil Nebula, part of the much larger Veil Nebula or Cygnus Loop.

Far more than simply a colourful cloud in space, the Veil is the remains of a massive star which exploded as a supernova around 10,000 to 20,000 years ago.

Modern measurements place the Cygnus Loop at approximately 2,420 light-years away, with the entire supernova remnant extending to around 120 light-years in diameter.

That means the beautiful wisps and filaments visible through modern astronomical equipment are the expanding debris of a stellar catastrophe which happened thousands of years before recorded history.

The practical evening formed part of Dr Alex MacKinnon's wider Exploring the Universe course, which is on offer as part of the adult education classes at West Kilbride.

Dr MacKinnon has previously given astronomy classes at Largs, and is a regular contributor to Inverclyde Skywatchers which meets in Inverkip on Mondays.
